comparisons.peer_topic: Accounting policy for government incentives recognition and classification
comparisons.peer_summary: Government incentives are recognized upon reasonable assurance of receipt and compliance, with capital-related incentives recorded as a reduction to property, plant, and equipment and operating-related incentives recorded as a reduction to the corresponding expense line item.
comparisons.comparison: Both MU and INTC disclose that government incentives are recorded as reductions to asset costs or operating expenses. MU states incentives are 'recorded... as a reduction of asset costs or a reduction of expenses,' while INTC specifies 'capital-related incentives as a reduction to property, plant, and equipment' and 'operating-related incentives as a reduction to expense.' INTC further details that capital-related incentives reduce depreciation expense, mirroring MU's treatment of incentives related to capital expenditures.

sentences.text: Government incentives are recorded in the financial statements in accordance with their purpose: as a reduction of asset costs or a reduction of expenses.

We record capital-related incentives as a reduction to property, plant, and equipment, net within our Consolidated Balance Sheets and recognize a reduction to depreciation expense over the useful life of the corresponding acquired asset.

We record operating-related incentives as a reduction to expense in the same line item on the Consolidated Statements of Operations as the expenditure for which the incentive is intended to compensate.

comparisons.peer_summary: Capital-related incentives reduced gross property, plant, and equipment by $9.5 billion as of December 28, 2024, with $4.1 billion recognized in 2024. These incentives reduced depreciation expense by $594 million in 2024, substantially all of which reduced cost of sales, and $3.3 billion of the total capital-related incentives recognized in 2024 was classified as a non-cash investing activity.
comparisons.comparison: While MU generally describes the cash flow classification of government incentives (operating for expenses, investing for PP&E), INTC provides specific quantitative impact on assets and depreciation, noting '$9.5 billion' reduction in gross PP&E and '$594 million' reduction in depreciation expense. INTC also explicitly classifies a portion of recognized capital incentives ($3.3 billion) as a 'non-cash investing activity,' which aligns with MU's policy of classifying cash received for PP&E incentives as an investing activity, though INTC's disclosure offers more granular financial impact data.

sentences.text: Cash received from government incentives related to operating expenses is included as an operating activity in the statement of cash flows, whereas cash received from incentives related to the acquisition of property, plant, and equipment is included as an investing activity.

Capital-related incentives reduced gross property, plant, and equipment by $9.5 billion as of December 28, 2024 ($5.5 billion as of December 30, 2023), of which $4.1 billion was recognized in 2024 ($2.2 billion in 2023).

Capital-related incentives reduced depreciation expense by $594 million in 2024, of which the substantial majority reduced cost of sales ($226 million in 2023, substantially all of which reduced cost of sales, and $230 million in 2022, all of which reduced cost of sales).
Of our total capital-related government incentives recognized in 2024, $3.3 billion was recognized as a non-cash investing activity ($1.1 billion in 2023 and $128 million in 2022).
